assumptions.statement: Households will regularly log and keep a pantry and fridge inventory current within the app.
assumptions.rationale: In-target working couples (1 of 1, P02:t8) state "Setup has to be fast. If I need to type in my whole pantry I'll quit on day two." Target families (2 of 3, P01:t10, P03:t10) insist it must work "without being a project" and "not making it feel like homework". Adjacent freelance couples (1 of 2, P05:t8) express the identical drop-off threat. If keeping an accurate inventory requires tedious manual data entry, users abandon tracking immediately and the core dinner planner fails completely.

assumptions.statement: Target households want and will follow a structured weekly dinner plan and consolidated weekly shopping list.
assumptions.rationale: A weekly plan fits weekly consolidated grocery shoppers such as target families (3 of 3, P01:t5, P03:t5, P04:t5). However, adjacent freelance and mobile couples (2 of 2, P05, P08) reject upfront weekly planning because dynamic schedules cause missed plans; P05:t1 notes "Planning ahead stresses me out. A plan I don't follow feels like failure, so I decide on the day" and P05:t4 abandoned a past app by Thursday. Daily shoppers (P05:t5, P09:t5) gain no utility from weekly lists. Sticking rigidly to a weekly calendar risks alienating households needing flexible same-day suggestions.

assumptions.statement: All households of two or more people cooking at home on weeknights suffer from dinner planning friction and food waste.
assumptions.rationale: The idea_brief assumes all multi-person households cooking weeknights share this struggle. While target families (2 of 3, P01:t2, P04:t2) and couples (1 of 1, P02:t2) report decision fatigue, target retired couples (1 of 1, P09:t1) report forty years of effortless daily routines with no planning burden ("Not much, honestly. Sometimes I'd like fresh ideas, but it isn't a problem", P09:t2). Even in target families, P03:t1 states "Planning is my favourite part of the week, honestly." Being in the demographic target does not mean having the problem.

assumptions.statement: Households will pay a monthly subscription for an inventory-integrated dinner planning app, and existing recipe apps do not solve this.
assumptions.rationale: The idea_brief claims existing apps do not know what you own, but this is contradicted by C:FridgeChef (fridge photo recognition), C:PantryGenie (barcode pantry tracking), and C:ZeroWaste Kitchen (leftover recipe matching). Median willingness to pay for cooking apps is EUR 3.50 per month (S05) and adoption is modest at 11% (S03). Target households state willingness to pay EUR 3 to EUR 6 only conditionally if grocery savings or waste reduction are proven (P01:t9, P04:t9), otherwise preferring free notes apps (P02:t9) or free versions (P03:t9, P05:t9, P09:t9).

assumptions.statement: Households experience dinner-table arguments and will adopt the app primarily to stop arguing about what is for dinner.
assumptions.rationale: The idea_brief pitches stopping dinner arguments. However, across all interviews, only 1 of 1 target couples mentions an argument (P02:t3: "argued for ten minutes about what to eat"). The primary recurring pain across target couples (1 of 1, P02:t4), target families (1 of 3, P04:t4), and adjacent flatmates (1 of 1, P10:t2) is multi-shopper coordination failure resulting in accidental duplicate purchases (buying chicken or basil twice) rather than emotional relationship conflict.

assumptions.statement: An automated planner can generate weeknight-realistic recipes under 30 minutes that utilize on-hand ingredients while respecting selective family preferences and allergies.
assumptions.rationale: Target families (2 of 3, P01:t8, P04:t8) explicitly require meals taking "Thirty minutes at most" and warn that the app must accommodate allergies and picky eaters: P04:t3 details cooking separate portions because children dislike sauces or peppers. If recommendations suggest complex recipes or fail dietary constraints, users will reject algorithmic suggestions as unusable noise.

experiments.hypothesis: At least 60% of busy target households will maintain a digital inventory across 7 days if given low-friction capture options (photo, barcode, or receipt import) rather than manual text entry.
experiments.method: Run a 7-day concierge test with 20 target households (10 busy families with school-age children, 10 dual-income working couples). Test four low-effort input methods (fridge shelf photo upload, receipt photo scanning, barcode scanning, and forward-forwarded online delivery order emails) without building the planner algorithm. Measure daily active item logging and self-reported friction.
experiments.success_metric: At least 12 of 20 households (60%) keep their inventory updated through day 7. If fewer than 50% persist past day 3, pivot away from full pantry tracking to perishable-only tracking or receipt-only imports.

experiments.hypothesis: Households with frequent or daily shopping habits achieve higher dinner-completion rates with same-day 'what can I cook tonight' suggestions than with upfront weekly plans.
experiments.method: Recruit 30 weeknight-cooking households segmented by shopping rhythm (15 consolidated weekly shoppers, 15 daily or irregular shoppers). Run a two-week Wizard of Oz split test: Week 1 gives both cohorts a rigid Sunday weekly meal calendar and grocery list; Week 2 gives both cohorts a 5 PM daily suggestion based on fridge ingredients. Track recipe completion, missed meals, and reported stress.
experiments.success_metric: If daily shoppers complete at least 40% more meals under same-day suggestions than under weekly plans, build same-day dynamic suggestions as a first-class feature rather than forcing a weekly schedule.

experiments.hypothesis: A value proposition centered on shopping coordination and waste savings achieves higher paid conversion at EUR 3.99 to EUR 4.99 per month than one pitched on stopping dinner arguments.
experiments.method: Run a multi-variant landing page smoke test targeting 600 qualifying household cooks. Variant A: 'Stop arguing about what is for dinner'; Variant B: 'Shared pantry and shopping list to prevent duplicate purchases'; Variant C: 'Cook what you already have and cut food waste'. Test call-to-action pre-orders at EUR 3.99/month and EUR 4.99/month (reflecting competitor anchors C:PantryGenie and C:SupperSync).
experiments.success_metric: A pre-order click conversion rate above 3% on Variant B or C at EUR 3.99/month, with Variant A underperforming by at least 30%. If conversion across all variants falls below 1.5%, reconsider subscription pricing in favor of freemium ad-supported models.

experiments.hypothesis: Screening for schedule variability and shared grocery friction identifies active problem sufferers with over 80% accuracy, whereas screening purely for multi-person households yields false positives.
experiments.method: Screen 40 weeknight-cooking households across three segments: 15 busy parents, 15 dual-income couples, and 10 retired couples. Administer a structured friction diagnostic measuring weekly food discarded, duplicate grocery occurrences, and late-afternoon decision fatigue.
experiments.success_metric: Over 75% of dual-income couples and busy parents report weekly waste or coordination failures, while retired couples report negligible friction (under 20%). Validates narrowing the target customer definition to exclude fixed-routine households.

open_questions: What are the geographic markets, household income levels, and recruitment channels of target households?
What is actual user retention and inventory update adherence beyond week one (longitudinal behavior)?
What are objectively measured household food waste quantities compared to self-reported estimates?

Which specific low-effort inventory input mechanism (fridge shelf photos, barcode scans, paper receipt OCR, or digital supermarket basket integration) delivers the highest completion rate and accuracy?
Do households sustain structured weekly dinner planning over time, or do they inevitably drift toward same-day improvisation?
What are the real market traction metrics (active subscriber counts, app store ratings, churn rates) of direct competitors such as C:MealLoop, C:SupperSync, C:FridgeChef, and C:PantryGenie?
What is the total addressable market size specifically for multi-person households experiencing weeknight dinner friction?
Within multi-person households, who holds the primary purchasing decision and who manages the daily cooking labor?
Can recipe generation algorithms reliably handle complex child allergies and selective eating under 30 minutes using only available pantry staples?
recommendation_reason: While genuine customer problems exist around late-afternoon decision fatigue (P01:t2, P04:t2, S04), perishable food spoilage (P01:t4, P02:t2, S01), and multi-shopper duplicate purchases (P02:t4, P04:t4), proceeding directly to build is blocked by severe unvalidated assumptions. Most critically, keeping an inventory up to date is the riskiest operational hurdle: participants explicitly warn that manual entry will make them quit on day two (P02:t8, P05:t8) and that the tool must not feel like homework (P03:t10). Furthermore, the core premise that existing apps do not know pantry inventory is contradicted by competitors (C:FridgeChef, C:PantryGenie), willingness to pay is low and strictly conditional (S05, P01:t9, P02:t9), and fixed weekly meal planning fails users with dynamic schedules (P05:t1, P05:t4). The team must test low-effort inventory input methods and compare weekly planning with same-day cooking suggestions before building the software.
